title: Should employers pay their employees better? An asset pricing approach

extraction.methodology_summary: The paper constructs a remuneration factor by sorting stocks within six supersectors based on their annual salaries and benefits expenses per employee. A market-neutral portfolio is formed daily by going long the highest-paying quantile and short the lowest-paying quantile, with weights scaled inversely by stock volatility and adjusted to ensure beta neutrality. The strategy's performance is evaluated using a novel 'Factor Correlation Level' (FCL) metric to measure common risk and compare it with other standard asset pricing factors.
extraction.universe: The 569 biggest companies in Europe, the 258 biggest companies on the London Stock Exchange, and 569 randomly selected U.S. companies with capitalization above 1 billion USD.

key_findings: Companies that spend more on salaries and benefits per employee (remuneration) perform better on the stock market on average.
Companies with similar remuneration policies share a common risk, which is comparable in magnitude to the value premium (book-to-market factor).
The remuneration anomaly is more pronounced for extreme quantiles (Q1) of the remuneration distribution.
The paper introduces the Factor Correlation Level (FCL) as a proxy for the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix to rank factors by importance.
The low-volatility factor is identified as the most important factor (highest FCL), followed by capitalization and momentum.
limitations: The methodology does not yield true eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the covariance matrix, meaning some inter-factor correlations remain (e.g., remuneration is correlated with sales-to-market and dividend factors).
Lack of systematic remuneration data for the U.S. universe prevented testing the remuneration factor on the U.S. market.
The study excludes microcapitalization firms, focusing only on liquid stocks with capitalization generally above 800 million euros.
